content.text: Weimar Germany: the hyperinflation crisis of 1923
By the end of this lesson I can
explain how reparations, the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr, passive resistance and printing money contributed to hyperinflation in Germany in 1923.
assess how hyperinflation affected different groups in Weimar Germany, including savers, wage earners and people with debts, using contemporary accounts and evidence of rising prices.
explain how Stresemann’s decision to end passive resistance and the introduction of the Rentenmark helped stabilise Germany’s economy in late 1923.
Why was the Ruhr occupied?
Reparations were payments Germany owed after the First World War.
Germany fell behind with deliveries of coal and timber.
In January 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied the industrial Ruhr to take goods instead.

slides.notes: Explain that the Ruhr was a major coal-producing and industrial region. Reparations were already putting pressure on Germany's finances; the occupation intensified an existing economic crisis. The photograph should show the occupation, not a generic First World War scene.

content.text: How did the crisis become hyperinflation?

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: The crisis escalates: Reparations deliveries fall behind, leads to, French and Belgian occupation, prompts, Passive resistance, reduces, Production and tax income, government responds

content.text: Passive resistance meant refusing to work for the occupying forces.
The government paid striking workers by printing more money.
With more money but fewer goods, prices rose rapidly: hyperinflation.

slides.notes: Read the chain aloud. At the fourth step, clarify that production and tax income fell. Germany had already been printing money before the occupation; paying for passive resistance made this worse. Printing notes did not create more coal, food or other goods. Falling confidence in the mark also accelerated price rises.

content.text: Why did printing money to fund passive resistance help cause hyperinflation?
Printing money created more goods.
Strikes increased Germany's tax income.
More money chased fewer available goods.
Reparations were paid to German workers.

slides.notes:
C. Passive resistance reduced production while the government printed more money to pay workers. More money chased fewer available goods, helping prices rise rapidly.
Ask everyone to choose an option before revealing the answer. If pupils choose A or B, revisit the difference between creating money and producing goods. Ask a pupil choosing C to connect occupation, passive resistance and printing money in a spoken explanation.

content.text: Who lost: and who could gain?
Savers
cash savings lost buying power. Debtors could repay fixed debts with money worth far less.
Wage earners
pay often lagged behind prices, so wages bought less.
Contemporary commentary
Keynes (1923) explained that inflation hurt fixed money incomes and benefited debtors. This is a paraphrase.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Reported Berlin bread prices, 1923: Month, Loaf price, January, 250 marks, September, 1.5 million marks, November, 200 billion marks

slides.notes: Prices are commonly reported examples for a loaf of bread in Berlin; actual prices varied by date, shop and loaf size. Do not present them as national monthly averages. The contemporary commentary is a paraphrase of J. M. Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform (1923), chapter I, discussing inflation's effects on different social groups. It is an economist's analysis, not a German worker's eyewitness testimony. Explain buying power as the amount of goods money can purchase. Fixed nominal debts could become easier to repay, but not every debtor benefited overall.

content.text: Quick check
Use the bread prices to explain why someone keeping savings in cash suffered.
Why might a wage earner suffer while someone with a fixed debt benefited? Use Keynes's analysis.
Do rising bread prices prove that every German was worse off? Explain.

slides.notes:
Give pupils brief thinking time and require evidence in their answers. Challenge the misconception that everyone lost equally. A person could belong to more than one group: for example, a wage earner might also have savings and debts.
Answers: 1. Bread rose from 250 marks to 200 billion marks. The same cash savings could therefore buy far less bread, so their buying power collapsed. 2. A wage earner suffered if pay rose more slowly than prices, because their wages bought less. A debtor could repay a fixed sum with money that was now worth much less. This supports Keynes's point that inflation affected groups differently. 3. No. They show that cash lost buying power, but effects depended on people's circumstances. Savers and many wage earners suffered, while some people with fixed debts benefited.

content.text: How did Stresemann restore stability?
September: Stresemann ended passive resistance, allowing production to restart and reducing government costs.
November: the Rentenmark replaced worthless paper marks for everyday use.
Its supply was limited and it was backed by land and industrial assets, helping restore confidence.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Two steps towards stability: 26 September 1923, Passive resistance ended, 15 November 1923, Rentenmark introduced

slides.notes: Explain that ending passive resistance reduced the need to pay striking workers and helped production resume. The Rentenmark was introduced under Stresemann's government: he did not personally design it alone. One Rentenmark equalled one trillion old paper marks. A new name alone was not enough; limiting currency issue and reducing government spending helped make the reform credible. Stability did not restore the savings people had already lost.

content.text: Quick check

Write three short paragraphs: explain how hyperinflation developed; assess its effects on savers, wage earners and debtors using the bread prices; explain how the two government responses helped stabilise the economy.

slides.notes:
Allow 6–8 minutes of silent independent writing. Keep the model answer hidden until pupils have finished. Check for causal links rather than a list of events, differences between groups, and explanations of both stabilisation measures. This also provides the first written check of objective 3.
Answers: 1. Germany fell behind with reparations deliveries, prompting French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr. Passive resistance reduced production and tax income. The government printed money to pay striking workers, helping drive rapid price rises. Bread rising from 250 marks to 200 billion marks shows how severely cash lost buying power. Savers lost the value of cash savings, and wage earners suffered when pay lagged behind prices. Some debtors benefited because fixed debts could be repaid with devalued money. Ending passive resistance reduced government costs and allowed production to restart. The limited supply of Rentenmarks helped restore confidence in money and stabilise prices.

content.text: Exit ticket
How did passive resistance and printing money combine to worsen inflation?
Explain one difference between the effects on cash savers and people with fixed debts.
Why did ending passive resistance and limiting the supply of Rentenmarks help stabilise the economy?

slides.notes:
Collect responses to identify whether pupils can explain mechanisms, rather than simply name events. Use errors to plan retrieval next lesson.
Answers: 1. Passive resistance reduced production while the government printed money to support striking workers. More money chasing fewer goods helped prices rise rapidly. 2. Cash savers lost buying power as prices rose. People with fixed debts could benefit by repaying the same nominal sum with money worth much less. 3. Ending passive resistance reduced government costs and helped production restart. Limiting the supply of the new currency helped restore confidence and prevented continued uncontrolled money creation.
